title: Troy (Hisarlık)
summary: A mound at Hisarlık near the Dardanelles holding superimposed settlements from about 3000 BCE to Byzantine times; its Late Bronze Age citadel is most probably the Hittites' Wilusa and the city of Homer's Iliad.
card: Troy is a layered settlement mound in northwest Türkiye whose levels, numbered Troy I to IX, span the Bronze Age and the Greek and Roman city of Ilion. In the Late Bronze Age a walled citadel of 2–3 ha stood here, and its excavators argue for a lower city of 25–35 ha around it, a claim critics have fiercely contested. Heinrich Schliemann's digs from 1870 made the site famous, damaged it badly, and produced the gold hoard now split between Berlin and Moscow.
what:
Troy is the archaeological site on the mound of Hisarlık in Çanakkale Province, northwestern Türkiye, about 4.8 km from the southern entrance to the Dardanelles. Its superimposed settlements, conventionally numbered Troy I to IX, begin about 3000 BCE and continue through the Bronze Age and the Greek and Roman city of Ilion into the late Byzantine period, giving archaeologists a reference sequence for the Aegean and Anatolia. Troy II, around 2500 BCE, had a fortified citadel with a paved ramp; the hoard Heinrich Schliemann named after King Priam came from this level, more than a thousand years before any possible Trojan War.

Troy VI, from about 1700 BCE, built a citadel of 2–3 ha inside walls of fitted limestone blocks more than 4 m thick, topped with mudbrick. Excavations led from 1988 by Manfred Korfmann found rock-cut ditches and a palisade about 400 m south of the citadel, which the excavators read as the defences of a lower city of 25–35 ha in Troy VI and VIIa. The end of Troy VIh is usually blamed on an earthquake; Troy VIIa, about 1250–1175 BCE, ended in fire.

Hittite texts name a western Anatolian kingdom, Wilusa, whose king Alaksandu concluded a treaty with Muwatalli II around 1280 BCE. Most specialists equate Wilusa with Greek Ilios and place it here, but the case rests on geography and names, since no archive has been found at the site. Greek Ilion grew on the ruins: Xerxes sacrificed to its Athena in 480 BCE, Alexander came in 334 BCE, and the terrace of a Hellenistic temple of Athena levelled the centre of the Bronze Age citadel.

Schliemann's campaigns of 1870–1890, begun on the advice of Frank Calvert, cut a trench about 14 m (45 ft) deep through the mound with little recording, destroying parts of the later levels in its path. Scholars disagree sharply about Late Bronze Age Troy: Frank Kolb and Dieter Hertel judged the lower city sparse and its reconstructions fiction, while the excavators and Easton, Hawkins and the Sherratts defended a regional capital. Whether the Iliad preserves a real war remains open.

uncertainty.note: Start is the conventional 'ca. 3000 BC' beginning of the Bronze Age sequence (Easton et al. 2002); UNESCO speaks of 4,000 years of history. Settlement continued into the late Byzantine period (Rose 2011; Jablonka & Rose 2004) and UNESCO notes Ottoman-period remains; no opened source gives a precise date for the end of habitation, so the end is set to the present, when the mound survives as a protected archaeological site (first excavated 1870; National Historical Park 1996; World Heritage 1998). Internal phase dates (Troy II c. 2500 BCE; Troy VI Late c. 1300–1250 BCE; VIIa c. 1250–1175 BCE) are pottery- and radiocarbon-based approximations.

how: Troy is a tell: each settlement was built on the levelled debris of the one before, on a limestone ridge rising from the alluvial plain near the mouth of the Dardanelles. The early citadels (Troy I–II) were walled and gated; after a cultural break, Troy VI introduced new architecture, grey wheelmade pottery and the first horses at the site. Its Late Bronze Age circuit wall was rebuilt section by section over generations in fitted limestone with a battered outer face, offsets and towers, on foundations deliberately left off bedrock, and fell at the end of VIh in what most excavators judge an earthquake. Troy VIIa rebuilt on the same plan and ended in fire about 1200–1175 BCE; VIIb shows new, Balkan-influenced material. Hittite texts locate Wilusa in the far west of the Arzawa lands, reached via the Seha River land, which points to the Troad. From the Archaic period Greek Ilion reused the ruins as a sanctuary city; Hellenistic builders sheared off the top of the mound for the temple terrace of Athena, and Hellenistic and Roman foundations, stone robbing, erosion and ploughing removed much of the Bronze Age lower city. Schliemann then trenched through the mound looking for a burned Homeric city, and later teams used stratigraphy, magnetic prospection and radiocarbon dating to rebuild the sequence.
why_it_matters: Troy is where the archaeology of the Aegean and Anatolia was given a datable backbone: UNESCO describes the chronology established by its excavations as fundamental to understanding the region's Bronze Age, and Schliemann's work there is often taken as the start of modern archaeology and of its public appeal. Its Late Bronze Age citadel and probable identification with Wilusa make it a meeting point of the Hittite and Mycenaean worlds, documented in Hittite diplomacy rather than in Greek epic alone. Its legend had concrete political consequences: Xerxes and Alexander staged sacrifices there, and Strabo records that Julius Caesar, claiming descent from Aeneas, granted Ilion territory, freedom and exemption from taxes, while the Aeneid turned the Trojan story into Rome's founding myth. Its modern history carries a live dispute, because the Troy II gold taken from Berlin in 1945 is held in Moscow under a 1998 Russian law that Berlin calls a breach of international law. A counterfactual shows what was lost: Jablonka and Rose argue that a city exchanging letters with Hittite kings must have kept an archive. Had Hellenistic temple builders not levelled the citadel's summit, and had Schliemann not trenched through what remained, the palace area and perhaps written records might have survived to settle whether Wilusa and Homer's Troy were the same place.

perspectives.holder: The Tübingen–Cincinnati excavators (Korfmann; Jablonka and Rose 2004) and Easton, Hawkins, Sherratt and Sherratt (2002)
perspectives.account: Late Bronze Age Troy (late VI and VIIa) was a citadel of 2–3 ha with a fortified lower city of 25–35 ha, defended by a rock-cut ditch and palisade, by far the largest site in the Troad and the probable capital of Wilusa with a significant role in regional exchange.

The lower city was only sparsely occupied in its middle and not at all in the south, the ditches were not defensive and were narrower than claimed, no lower-town wall has been shown, and the population should be put at 3,000 or even 1,000; Kolb also holds that Troy's trade role is unproven and that the reconstructions mix findings with assumption.

perspectives.holder: Hittitologists such as J. D. Hawkins and F. Starke (as reported by Easton et al. 2002), followed by Livius
perspectives.account: Hittite geography places the Arzawa kingdom of Wilusa in the Troad, and Hisarlık is the only site there of the right rank, so Wilusa is most probably Troy/Ilios; S. Heinhold-Krahmer treated this as unproven, and Hertel denied it.

perspectives.holder: Blegen's excavators and later analysts summarised by Rutter and Livius
perspectives.account: Troy VI was destroyed by an earthquake and Troy VIIa was sacked, but VIIa's fall came when Mycenaean palaces could hardly mount an overseas expedition, so the Iliad does not straightforwardly describe a datable event; Smithsonian Magazine instead reports a general view placing the epic's events at Hisarlık around 1180 BCE.

perspectives.holder: Strabo (1st century BCE), following Demetrius of Scepsis
perspectives.account: The Ilion of his day was not the site of Homer's Ilium when the poems' geography is taken at face value.

perspectives.holder: Staatliche Museen zu Berlin (German position on 'Priam's Treasure')
perspectives.account: Schliemann gave the collection to Berlin in 1881; the Red Army took the gold as spoils of war in 1945; the 1998 Duma resolution declaring it Russian state property contravenes international law, and Berlin remains custodian of the collection under his bequest.

perspectives.holder: Russian museum and public view as reported in 1996 (Pushkin Museum exhibition)
perspectives.account: Many Russians regard the gold as legitimately taken spoils of victory over Nazi Germany; the Pushkin Museum put it on display from 15 April 1996 despite German objections.

phases.description: Troy I walled settlement; a stretch of its earliest wall survives near the south gate.
Troy II fortified citadel with paved ramp and a rock-cut palisade and gate about 150 m south; source of the 1873 hoard.

Troy VI begins about 1700 BCE (Livius); early and middle citadel walls with gates VI Z, VI Y and VI T (Rutter); inner lower-city ditch cut in Troy VI Middle, about the 15th century BCE (Jablonka and Rose).
Late Troy VI circuit wall rebuilt section by section from Troy VIf (about 1400 BCE), towers VI h and VI i added in VIh; lower city with ditch and palisade.
End of Troy VIh, most often attributed to a severe earthquake (timing within Troy VI Late, about 1300–1250 BCE).
Troy VIIa: denser houses inside the old walls, mudbrick on a massive stone foundation at the Northeast Bastion, outer ditch; ends in fire.
Troy VIIb: rebuilt houses and huts with new material culture; abandoned in the early 10th century BCE while walls still stood.
Greek Ilion as a sanctuary village with a small temple of Athena (Strabo); Xerxes sacrifices to Athena of Ilium on the 480 BCE campaign.
Hellenistic Ilion: new temple of Athena built after Alexander's visit; its terrace destroys the centre of the Late Bronze Age citadel.
Fimbria takes Ilion by siege on the eleventh day during the First Mithridatic War (85 BCE).
Roman Ilion restored under Sulla and Caesar; odeion and bouleuterion on the edge of the agora survive almost complete.
An earthquake around 500 CE ends Ilion's prosperity (Livius); reduced occupation continues into the late Byzantine period (Rose 2011), with Ottoman-period remains also attested.
Schliemann's excavations cut a trench about 14 m deep through the mound with little recording, destroying parts of the levels in its path.
Excavations by Dörpfeld (1893–1894), Blegen (1932–1938) and the Tübingen–Cincinnati project (1987/88–2012); limited anastylosis of the defences.
World Heritage property (158 ha); Turkish excavations (Ministry of Culture and Tourism with Çanakkale Onsekiz Mart University) reported a Late Bronze Age open square in 2026.
